origin_region: Chiayi · Alishan and Nantou · Mingjian (grown island-wide)
processing: Lightly oxidised (roughly 15–25%), ball-rolled and dried with little or no roast; a light roast is sometimes applied to lowland lots. Nothing is added: the creamy note is natural to the cultivar.
harvest_season: Spring (April–May) and winter (October–November) are the premium pickings, especially from Alishan; lowland gardens in Mingjian pick it several times a year and sell summer and autumn lots cheaply.
appearance_dry: Plump, tightly rolled green balls, a little larger and rounder than Qing Xin, with yellow-green stems.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow with a soft green tint, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Broad, rounded, bright-green leaves on thick stems, opening fully by the third steep.
taste_profile: Butter, sweet corn and a milky texture with soft osmanthus-like florals and a clean sweet finish; at altitude it gains thickness and a cooling aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Forgiving: water just off the boil, moderate steeps, five or six good infusions. One of the best teas for cold brewing (about 1 g per 100 ml, overnight in the fridge), where the creaminess comes forward.

vintage_note: Sold by cultivar name, growing area and season: Alishan Jin Xuan from the spring and winter harvests of the current year is the top of the range, while Mingjian lowland Jin Xuan is sold year-round, often with no season stated. It is a fresh tea for drinking within a year. Flavoured 'milk oolong' follows no vintage logic at all, which is one way to spot it.
description:
Jin Xuan is a Taiwanese tea cultivar, Taiwan Tea Experiment Station number 12, released in 1981 and now the second most planted bush on the island after Qing Xin. It is the real thing behind 'milk oolong': the leaf has a natural buttery, creamy note with a touch of osmanthus, without anything being added to it. It grows everywhere from the Mingjian lowlands to Alishan at 1,500 metres, and Alishan Jin Xuan is the version most worth seeking out.

The cultivar was bred at the research station under Wu Zhenduo from a cross between a station breeding line (Tainong 8) and the local Ying Zhi Hong Xin bush, and is said to carry his grandmother's name. It yields noticeably more than Qing Xin and shrugs off disease, which is why farmers took to it. The leaf is larger and rounder than Qing Xin and is usually made as a lightly oxidised, ball-rolled oolong with little or no roast; the same leaf also turns up as Jin Xuan black tea and in bug-bitten honey styles.

In the cup, expect butter, sweet corn and a milky texture, with soft florals and a clean, sweet finish; at altitude it gains thickness and a cooling aftertaste, in the lowlands it stays simple and pleasant. It is forgiving to brew: water just off the boil, moderate steeps, and it gives five or six good infusions. It is also one of the best teas for cold brewing, where the creaminess comes forward.

The trap is flavoured 'milk oolong'. A great deal of what is sold under that name, especially from mainland China and Thailand, is low-grade rolled oolong sprayed with milk flavouring; if the dry leaf smells like condensed milk, or the aroma survives five steeps unchanged, it is flavoured. Genuine Jin Xuan is subtle: the creaminess is a texture and a hint, not a dessert. Buy it by cultivar name and season, spring or winter, from a seller who names the growing area.

If you like it, Cui Yu (number 13), its sister cultivar from the same year, is the floral counterpart, and Jin Xuan black shows the same leaf fully oxidised.
sources_note: Parentage given as Tainong 8 line x Ying Zhi Hong Xin from memory of TRES cultivar notes; the 'named after Wu Zhenduo's grandmother' story is widely repeated but anecdotal.
